title: Exploring the Role of Drug-Induced Sleep Endoscopy in Optimizing Upper Airway Stimulation Therapy for Non-Responders
authors: Kant E, Hardeman JA, Stokroos RJ, Copper MP.
blurb: Kant and colleagues reviewed 29 non-responders to Inspire upper airway stimulation who underwent drug-induced sleep endoscopy with the device switched on, to guide changes in stimulation settings or additional treatment. Among the 18 patients with follow-up, 8 became responders, mostly after device-setting changes or barbed reposition pharyngoplasty, but there was no control group and, as the authors note, more than half were not effectively treated. The call is watch: it is a reasonable option for tolerant non-responders, but it is not yet proven to add benefit.

title: Oropharyngeal Lateral Wall Collapse on Drug-Induced Sleep Endoscopy as a Predictor of Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation Response in Obstructive Sleep Apnoea-A Systematic Review
authors: McBrinn S, Skan O, Iacovidou A.
blurb: A systematic review of eight Inspire cohorts, 1,051 patients in all, asked whether complete collapse of the lateral pharyngeal walls on sleep endoscopy predicts a poor response to hypoglossal nerve stimulation. It lowers the response rate by roughly 15 to 20 percentage points, yet about two of three such patients still respond, so it is a counseling point rather than an exclusion. Call: watch.

title: Edema and Subjective Discomfort After Barbed Stayed Bridge Pharyngoplasty (BSBP)
authors: Pace A, Iannella G, Maniaci A, Cocuzza S, Moffa A, Alunni Fegatelli D, et al.
blurb: A prospective Italian cohort scored palatal swelling and discomfort day by day after barbed stayed bridge pharyngoplasty, a variant of barbed palate surgery. Swelling and pain peaked in the first day and improved markedly by 48 hours, which sharpens recovery counseling, but the technique was not compared with standard barbed reposition pharyngoplasty. Call: watch; no change in technique.

title: Consensus Statements Among European Sleep Surgery Experts on Tongue, Hypopharynx, and Supraglottis Associated With Snoring and Obstructive Sleep Apnea - Part 1 - Evaluation and Decision Making
authors: Olszewska E, De Vito A, Baptista P, Delakorda M, Heiser C, Cheong RCT, et al.
blurb: A European expert panel reached consensus on how to evaluate the tongue base, hypopharynx and supraglottis in snoring and sleep apnea, and how those findings should steer treatment. The statements support staging palate surgery before hypoglossal nerve stimulation when large tonsils coexist with tongue base collapse, and repeating sleep endoscopy before any revision surgery. Call: watch; the workup stays as it is.
